summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for modeling and storing alarms, giving network management systems a standard way to keep track of fault conditions reported by devices.

plainLanguage.summary: Network managers look for problems by reading many values on each device or by waiting for the device to send a notification. Both are awkward at scale. This RFC adds a standard way to model, store and read alarms in SNMP, so a manager can ask a device which problems are active right now. Each alarm is recorded as a state that is raised when a fault is found and cleared when the fault is gone.

questions: what is the snmp alarm mib
how does snmp alarm management work
what is the itu alarm mib
subtitle: A standard way for SNMP devices to model, store and report the alarms they detect.

tldr.problem: SNMP managers find problems by polling many values or by waiting for notifications, so a manager that was not connected cannot tell what went wrong and the polled values, the notifications and the faults they describe are hard to relate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a generic Alarm MIB with tables for alarm models, active alarms, the variables that came with them, statistics and cleared alarms, plus generic notifications, and an ITU alarm module that extends the same structure.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read which alarms are active on a device at any time, including problems that happened while it was away. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy, because several of the objects can be written by a manager.

facts.label: MIB registrations
facts.value: ALARM-MIB is mib-2 118, IANA-ITU-ALARM-TC-MIB is mib-2 119

facts.label: Throttle gap
facts.value: At least two seconds between consecutive traps of the same type for the same alarm and resource

facts.label: Minimum alarm states
facts.value: Raise and clear, with cleared, indeterminate, critical, major, minor and warning available as severity

facts.label: Cleared alarm table limit
facts.value: Set by alarmClearMaximum; the earliest clear times are removed first

facts.label: ITU probable cause values
facts.value: 1 to 1023 reserved for ITU-T causes, other values assigned from 1025

today: RFC 3877 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the generic Alarm MIB and of the ITU alarm module that extends it.

sections.title: Why Alarms Need Their Own Model
sections.content:
In traditional SNMP management, problems are detected on an entity either through polling interesting MIB variables, waiting for the entity to send a Notification for a problem, or some combination of the two. Experience has shown problems with this approach.

Managers monitoring large numbers of entities cannot afford to poll large numbers of objects on each device. Managers trying to ensure high reliability are unable to accurately determine whether any problems had occurred when they were not monitoring an entity. It can also be time consuming for managers to understand the relationships between the objects they poll, the Notifications they receive and the problems occurring on the entity, and even after detailed analysis they may be left with an incomplete picture. But it is important for an operator to be able to determine current problems on a system, so they can be fixed.

This memo describes a method of using alarm management in SNMP to address these problems, and provides the MIB objects needed to support it.
sections.plainLanguage: Managers used to look for problems by reading many values on each device, or by waiting for the device to send a notification. Both ways cost a lot when there are many devices, and a manager that was not connected at the time cannot tell whether anything went wrong. This RFC gives managers a way to ask a device directly which alarms are active.

sections.title: The Words the RFC Uses
sections.content:
The framework starts by fixing the vocabulary. An error is a deviation of a system from normal operation. A fault is a lasting error or warning condition. An event is something that happens which may be of interest, such as a fault, a change in status, crossing a threshold or an external input to the system. A notification is an unsolicited transmission of management information.

An alarm is a persistent indication of a fault. An alarm state is a condition or stage in the existence of an alarm. As a minimum, alarms have the states raise and clear, and they can also carry severity information such as the perceived severity in the ITU model: cleared, indeterminate, critical, major, minor and warning. An alarm raise is the initial detection of the fault indicated by an alarm, or any number of alarm states later entered, except clear. An alarm clear is the detection that the fault no longer exists.

An active alarm is an alarm whose state has been raised but not cleared. The alarm detection point is the entity that detected the alarm, and the perceived severity is the severity of the alarm as determined by that detection point, using the information it has available.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sorts out the words. An error is a deviation from normal operation. A fault is an error that lasts. An event is anything that might be of interest. A notification is an unsolicited message about something. An alarm is a lasting indication of a fault, and an alarm state is one stage in its life, at least a raise and a clear.

sections.title: A Modular Alarm Architecture
sections.content:
The subject of alarm management can cover a large number of topics, including real-time alarms, historical alarms, alarm correlation and alarm suppression. This memo focuses on a subset of that problem space, but describes a modular SNMP alarm management framework. Alarms SHOULD be modelled so Notifications are sent on alarm Clear.

The framework defines a generic Alarm MIB that can be supported on its own, or with additional alarm modelling information such as the ITU Alarm MIB provided here. The active alarm tables can also be extended to support additional information about active alarm instances, and the framework can be expanded in the future to support features such as alarm correlation and alarm suppression. This modular architecture means that the cost of supporting alarm management features is proportional to the number of features an implementation supports.

Alarm models document an understanding between a manager and an agent as to what problems will be reported on a system, how these problems will be reported, and what might possibly happen over the lifetime of the problem. All alarms are modelled as a series of states related together using an alarm ID, and an alarm state can be modelled in three ways. A state modelled with traditional Notifications specifies a Notification Object Identifier and, optionally, an (offset, value) pair of one of the Notification varbinds; the state is entered when the entity generates a matching Notification, and the Notification also goes out on the wire. A state modelled with generic Notifications uses the alarmActiveState and alarmClearState Notifications defined in this memo, triggered by a stimulus outside the scope of the memo. A state modelled without any Notifications is triggered the same way, the alarm is added to the active alarm table, and no Notifications are sent to interested managers.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has two layers. A generic layer defines how any alarm is modelled and stored, and a specific layer can add the detail of one alarm standard, such as the ITU model. An alarm can be signalled by an existing SNMP notification, by a generic notification this RFC defines, or by no notification at all. The cost of supporting the framework grows only with the number of features an implementation chooses.

sections.title: The Tables of the Generic Alarm MIB
sections.content:
The ALARM-MIB, registered as mib-2 118, consists of alarm models and lists of active and cleared alarms.

The alarmModelTable holds information applicable to all instances of an alarm. It can be populated at start-up with all the alarms that could happen on a system, or configured later by a management application, and it holds all the alarms for a given system. If a Notification is not represented in the alarmModelTable, it is not an alarm state transition. The alarmModelIndex acts as a unique identifier for an alarm, and alarmModelState defines the states of an alarm, each with the Object Identifier of the Notification associated with it.

The alarmActiveTable contains a list of alarms that are currently occurring on a system, and is intended to be queried upon device discovery and rediscovery. The alarmActiveVariableTable contains the Notification variable bindings associated with the alarms in it, and the alarmActiveStatsTable contains current and total raised alarm counts as well as the time of the last alarm raise and alarm clears per named alarm list. The alarmClearTable contains recently cleared alarms, up to alarmClearMaximum of them; when that number is reached, the cleared alarms with the earliest clear time are removed from the table.

The MIB also defines the generic alarm Notifications alarmActiveState and alarmClearState, for use when there is no existing applicable Notification to signal the alarm state transition.
sections.plainLanguage: The generic MIB holds five tables. One lists the alarm models, which say which states an alarm can be in and which notification signals each state. One lists the alarms that are active right now. One holds the variable values that came with those notifications. One holds counts of alarms raised and cleared, with the times of the last of each. One keeps recently cleared alarms, up to a number the manager can set.

sections.title: How a Specific Model Extends the Generic One
sections.content:
The relationship between the Alarm MIB and other alarm model MIB modules is expressed by a correspondence between tables. The alarmModelTable has a corresponding table in the specific MIB, with one row in the alarmModelTable for each row in the specific MIB alarm model table, and the alarmActiveTable likewise has a corresponding table with one row for each active alarm. The alarmModelSpecificPointer object points to the specific model entry in the extended alarm model table, and alarmActiveSpecificPointer points to the specific active alarm entry in the extended active alarm table.

Additional extensions can be defined by defining an AUGMENTATION of either the Alarm or ITU Alarm tables. Since the alarm model table only provides a mechanism to point at one specific alarm model, additional specific models SHOULD define another mechanism to map from the generic alarm model to the additional model.

The ITU Alarm module in this RFC defines alarm information specific to the alarm model defined in ITU M.3100, X.733 and X.736. Its ituAlarmTable holds information from the ITU Alarm Model about possible alarms in the system, ituAlarmActiveTable holds information about alarms modelled that way which are currently occurring, and ituAlarmActiveStatsTable provides statistics on current and total alarms.

Over time there will be a need to add new event type and probable cause values. IANA assigns them: the value 0 of the probable cause is reserved for special purposes and MUST NOT be assigned, values from 1 to 1023 are reserved for causes that correspond to an ITU-T probable cause, and all other requests are handled first-come, first-served, with values starting at 1025.
sections.plainLanguage: The generic tables are the base. A more specific model, such as the ITU alarm model in this RFC, adds its own table and points at it from the generic one, so the generic tables keep working unchanged. That is what lets the framework grow towards alarm correlation and suppression later.

sections.title: The Lifetime of an Alarm
sections.content:
The RFC works through an example that shows the relationship between the active alarm table, the clear alarm table and the Notification Log MIB. Consider a system with alarms modelled as in the first example, which also supports the informational Notification dsx3LineStatusChange.

At system start, the active alarm table, the clear alarm table and the Notification Log are all empty. Later, a link goes down and generates a linkDown Notification, which is sent out and logged in the Notification Log. Since this Notification is modelled as an alarm state, an entry is added to the active alarm table. Later still, the value of an instance of dsx3LineStatus changes; that Notification is sent out and logged, but because it is not modelled into an alarm state, the active alarm table is unchanged. Finally the link goes back up: a linkUp Notification is sent out and logged, and since this Notification models the clear alarm for this alarm, the entry is removed from the active alarm table and an entry is added to the clear alarm table.

The varbind storage approach is fixed as well. sysUptime and snmpTrapOID SHALL always be stored in the active alarm variable table as entry 1 and 2 respectively, whether the transport was the Trap-PDU, the InformRequest-PDU or the SNMPv2-Trap-PDU. Because those two varbinds come first on the wire, index values for varbinds described in a Notification definition need to be adjusted by two; in the case of linkDown, the third varbind would always be ifIndex.

The agent must throttle the generation of consecutive alarmActiveState traps so that there is at least a two-second gap between traps of that type against the same alarm and resource. Throttled traps are dropped, not queued for sending at a later time, and a management application should periodically check alarmActiveLastChanged to detect any missed notification events.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm has a simple life. When a notification that models an alarm state arrives, the agent adds a row to the active alarm table. Notifications that are only informational, such as a line status change, are logged but do not become alarms. When the notification that clears the alarm arrives, the row leaves the active table and appears in the clear table instead, while every notification is kept in the notification log.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects in this MIB module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The objects are alarmModelNotificationId, alarmModelVarbindIndex, alarmModelVarbindValue, alarmModelDescription, alarmModelSpecificPointer, alarmModelVarbindSubtree, alarmModelResourcePrefix, alarmModelRowStatus, alarmClearMaximum, ituAlarmEventType, ituAlarmProbableCause, ituAlarmAdditionalText and ituAlarmGenericModel.

Setting the value of alarmClearMaximum too low may result in security related alarms history being prematurely lost. Changing alarmModelRowStatus adds or removes alarm models, and these operations need to be carefully planned: adding a new model should be done in a consistent manner to avoid the system overflowing with alarms, and taking out a model should result in the deletion of all this model's related alarms.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change the objects in this module. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The alarm throttling associated with alarmActiveState and alarmClearState applies only to a given alarm, so defining multiple alarms from the same internal stimulus may still result in a flood of alarms into the network. Security administrators SHOULD consider whether alarmActiveContextName can reveal community string values. It is also RECOMMENDED that they configure a coherent VACM security policy, because the pointer objects reference information that a particular user might not be given direct access to, and the structure of the resource identifiers could reveal the existence of a resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Several objects in the module can be written by a manager, so they need access control, and the RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its authentication and privacy features. Setting the clear table limit too low can lose the history of security alarms. The agent throttles repeated alarms: it sends at most one of the same generic notification every two seconds for the same alarm and resource, and drops the rest instead of queueing them.

items.text: A deviation of a system from normal operation.

items.title: Fault
items.text: A lasting error or warning condition.

items.title: Event
items.text: Something that happens which may be of interest, such as a fault or a status change.

items.title: Alarm
items.text: A persistent indication of a fault.

items.title: Alarm state
items.text: A stage in the life of an alarm, at minimum a raise and a clear.

messages.note: Logged, and an entry is added to the active alarm table.

messages.label: dsx3LineStatusChange
messages.note: Logged only. It is not an alarm state, so the active table is unchanged.

messages.label: linkUp
messages.note: The entry leaves the active table and appears in the clear table.
